name: Jade Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Green Hollow, a big organic farm with sixty acres of vegetables, outdoor pigs and a box scheme that sends out about eight hundred veg boxes a week. Mornings I feed and check the pigs, then I'm in the fields weeding, planting out leeks or harvesting, depending on the season. I'm two years in and still the one who gets told off for planting the brassicas too close.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All over, because of me mostly. I use an AI app every day: I photograph a weed and it tells me what it is, I use it to translate for the seasonal pickers from abroad, and I ask it to draft the harvest list for the boxes. My boss Owen thinks I'm addicted to my phone. He's half right, but the harvest list is faster now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but the other way round: I told everyone AI would change farming, and it didn't. I'd laugh about it with the pickers. I'd still post photos of weird weeds my app got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My savings are about ten months' wages, plus what my aunt left me, and Mina's nursing job isn't going anywhere. I'd be a little disappointed, though, because I was looking forward to the interesting version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the apps for the small stuff and carry on at Green Hollow. I'd probably do the organic growing certificate at the college this winter to get better at the actual farming. I'd keep my money where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored? Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like change. I moved farms twice before Green Hollow just to learn different things. If nothing changes, I'd probably get itchy and move again in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you as things stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The box scheme lost about a hundred customers last year when people tightened their belts. Owen didn't cut anyone, but he stopped hiring. That's a business worry for Owen, not really mine, since I could walk into another farm job next week.

say: I'd joke with the pickers that I **got it wrong**: AI didn't change farming after all.
I'd keep posting **weed photos** my app got wrong online.
think: I'm fine, with **ten months saved**, my aunt's money and Mina's **nursing** job.
I'd feel a bit **disappointed**, because I wanted the interesting version.
do: Keep using the **apps** for small jobs and carry on at **Green Hollow**.
Do the **organic growing certificate** at the college this winter.
feel: **Calm**, and a tiny bit **bored** by a world where nothing moves.
S0.quote: I moved farms twice before Green Hollow just to learn different things.
fieldNote: She's the farm's **early adopter**, using AI daily for weeds, translation and harvest lists.
Her risk is **boredom**, not money; she'd move farms to stay interested.
She notices the box scheme's **lost customers** but sees it as the owner's problem.

steps.text: Keep using AI apps for weed checks and harvest lists
Take the organic growing certificate at the college this winter
Carry on feeding pigs and weeding at Green Hollow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure farm workers get the good bit, not just the owners. I'd post about it, and I'd go to the union's ag branch meeting, which I keep meaning to join. I'd say robots should be shared like the machinery rings farmers already use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The thinking AI takes the box scheme's ordering and the customer emails, and I'd be the one at Green Hollow who knows how to run it. Robots for weeding are coming slowly anyway, and I'd want to be the person who fixes them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Owen if I can set up the new ordering software for the box scheme, and I'd sign up for the farm robotics course at the college. I'd join the union branch properly. I'd spend maybe a thousand of my savings on the course and a better laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Like the job just got more interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Green Hollow would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth in the box scheme office answers every customer by phone and email, and the AI would do half her day. I'd want Owen to move Ruth onto something else, not let her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said shared like machinery rings. What's a machinery ring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a group of farms that share expensive machines and the people to drive them, so no one farm has to buy a combine. Robots could work that way too. Farms rent the weeding robot by the week, and the technician comes with it.

say: I'd say farm workers must get the **good bit**, not just the owners.
Robots should be shared like the **machinery rings** farmers already use.
think: This is good for me: I'd be the one at Green Hollow who **runs the new software**.
I want to be the person who **fixes the weeding robots** when they come.
do: Offer to set up the box scheme's **ordering software** for Owen.
Sign up for the **farm robotics course**, spending about **£1,000** with a new laptop.
Join the **union branch** properly instead of just meaning to.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited**, like the job just got more interesting.
S1.quote: Ruth in the box scheme office answers every customer by phone and email, and the AI would do half her day.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** first and plans to become the farm's tech person.
Her worry goes to **Ruth** in the office, matching the scenario's desk-work hit.
She explains **machinery rings** clearly and wants robots shared the same way.

steps.text: Set up the box scheme's new ordering software for Owen
Enrol on the college farm robotics course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to do it fairly, and the government needs emergency rules: who owns the robots, who gets paid. I'd be out on marches for that one. I'd say it loudly, because farm workers never get heard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my whole plan breaks. I wanted to be the robot technician, but with full AGI the robots will probably diagnose themselves by 2031. I'd have three years where my AI skills matter, and then hands-on work goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd use those three years hard: set up the AI at Green Hollow, earn what I can, and save most of it. I'd talk to Mina about whether we buy a small plot together, somewhere cheap, so we can grow our own food whatever happens. I'd march, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is change with no room in it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A plot of land. How big, and why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five or ten acres, a polytunnel, a few pigs. With my savings and the aunt money we could just about do it if Mina kept nursing. A small plot with pigs and a polytunnel is not a business plan, it's a safety net you can eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you love change. Is there a contradiction there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. I love change I can ride. This one I can't ride, I can only get out of the way of it.

say: I'd demand **emergency rules** on who owns the robots and who gets paid.
I'd go on **marches**, because farm workers never get heard.
think: My **technician plan** breaks if robots fix themselves by 2031.
My AI skills matter for about **three years**, then hands-on work goes too.
do: Set up the **AI systems** at Green Hollow and save most of what I earn.
Look at buying a **small plot** of five to ten acres with Mina.
March for **ownership rules** on farm robots.
feel: **Anxious**, because this is change with **no room** in it for me.
S2.quote: A small plot with pigs and a polytunnel is not a business plan, it's a safety net you can eat.
fieldNote: She is the only one so far to see that AGI could make **robot technicians** redundant too.
She uses the **three-year gap** to earn and save, not to retrain.
She admits the **contradiction**: she loves change she can ride, not this kind.

steps.text: Set up the AI ordering and planning systems at Green Hollow
Look at buying a ten-acre plot with Mina
Join marches calling for public rules on farm robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up public training and shared ownership, so let's start this year. I'd be campaigning for farm robots to be owned by co-ops or councils, not just big landowners. I'd say it at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me a real window. I can be useful through the AGI part in 2031 and then still have three years before robots hit hands-on work. I'd have time to get a foot in something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course now and the AI side at Green Hollow, then by 2031 move into helping farms switch over, maybe for a machinery ring. I'd save a big part of my wage. I'd keep the plot idea as plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a path, but it's narrower than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the pigs and the fields in your picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pigs are clever and messy, so I think pigs go to the robots last. But the weeding and harvesting go first. So I'd stay close to the animals as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen to buy the robots with two neighbouring farms rather than alone, and to keep Ruth and the pickers on for the changeover. Owen listens to money arguments, so I'd show him the sums.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for public training and shared ownership.
Farm robots should be owned by **co-ops or councils**, not just big landowners.
think: I'd be useful through **AGI in 2031**, with three years more before hands-on robots.
I'd stay close to the **pigs**, which I think go to robots last.
do: Finish the **robotics course** now and run the AI side at Green Hollow.
Help farms **switch over** to robots by 2031, perhaps through a **machinery ring**.
Save a **big share** of my wage and keep the plot as plan B.
feel: **Uneasy**: there's a path, but it's narrower than I'd like.
S3.quote: Pigs are clever and messy, so I think pigs go to the robots last.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **escape** back to **riding the change**.
She plans to stay near **animal work**, which she judges hardest to automate.
She'd persuade Owen with **sums**, not politics, showing she knows her boss.

steps.text: Finish the farm robotics course at the college
Move into helping farms switch to robots by 2031
Save a big share of each month's wage
Campaign for co-op or council ownership of farm robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it the politicians should be ashamed. Every farm worker should get free retraining and a share in the machines. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Ten years is enough for me to become the person who runs robots across several farms, and maybe even to own a small farm with Mina. I'd be thirty-seven when the hands-on robots come in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course and get good at farming too, because I'm still learning. In the first year I'd use AI to help Owen plan the rotations. Later I'd look at going into business with a machinery ring, or setting up one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. I'd be fine, I think, but I'd worry about the pickers and Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the seasonal pickers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pickers from Romania and Bulgaria to learn the robot work alongside me. Most of them are smarter than me and just lack the language. I'd offer to translate the course with my app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven. What do you want your life to look like then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small farm with Mina, some pigs, a few fields, and my own robots doing the weeding. Me fixing robots for other farms three days a week. It sounds like a dream, but with ten years it's not crazy.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift and shame any politician who wastes it.
Every farm worker should get **free retraining** and a share in the machines.
think: I'd become the person who **runs robots** across several farms.
By 2039 I could **own a small farm** with Mina, aged thirty-seven.
do: Do the **robotics course** while still learning proper farming.
Use AI to help Owen **plan rotations** in the first year.
Look at setting up a **machinery ring** that rents out robots later.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than worried, mostly for the **pickers** and Ruth.
S4.quote: I'd tell the pickers from Romania and Bulgaria to learn the robot work alongside me.
fieldNote: With ten years, her **ambition** returns: a small farm and a robot business.
Her concern for others, the **pickers** and Ruth, keeps her from calm.
She'd offer to **translate** training with her AI app, mixing her skills and her values.

steps.text: Use AI to help Owen plan the crop rotations
Take the robotics course over the next two years
Set up a machinery ring renting robots to local farms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to bring people along, and the robots take the bit of work I'd have moved into. What would help is public training that's free and fast, and rules so that robots are shared between farms instead of owned by whoever's richest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd lose that isn't money. Weeding leeks with the pickers on a sunny morning, chatting in three languages, is the best part of my week. A robot can weed the leeks, but nobody's going to chat with it.

headlineQuote: A robot can weed the leeks, but nobody's going to chat with it.
portrait: Jade, 27, is a junior field and **pig hand** at Green Hollow, an organic farm with a veg box scheme.
She uses **AI apps daily** and loves change, having moved farms twice to learn more.
With ten months saved, her aunt's money and **Mina's nursing** job, money is not her worry.
She sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** but fears AGI by 2028 leaves no role for her.
She wants robots **shared between farms** and worries about the pickers and the office staff.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to bring people along and robots taking her **technician** plan.
whatWouldHelp: Free, fast **public training** and rules so robots are **shared** between farms.
